summary: Defines a new option for the Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol (MADCAP) so that nested multicast scopes can be described. This lets a client learn how one multicast scope sits inside another. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Some addresses are for talking to a group. Groups can sit inside bigger groups, like a classroom inside a school. This lets a computer learn which group sits inside which.

questions: what is the madcap multicast scope nesting state option
what is the split horizon effect in multicast ttl scoping
what is an expanding scope search
how is multicast scope nesting encoded
subtitle: A MADCAP option that tells clients which multicast scopes sit inside which, so they can widen a search one scope at a time.

tldr.problem: MADCAP clients can learn which multicast scopes exist, but not how they nest inside each other, which they need for expanding scope searches and hierarchical multicast transport.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional option, code 17, carries a bit-packed matrix in which a 1 means the row scope nests inside the column scope, and servers keep the state fresh with two timers.
tldr.outcome: Clients can pick better scopes and widen a search one nesting level at a time, avoiding the split horizon effect of TTL-based searches.

today: RFC 2907 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The option is OPTIONAL for MADCAP servers, and IANA has assigned it option code 17.

sections.title: What the Option Adds to MADCAP
sections.content:
The Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol (MADCAP, RFC 2730) lets clients ask multicast address allocation servers to reserve, request and extend leases on multicast addresses. It is part of the Multicast Address Allocation Architecture (RFC 2908).

MADCAP's existing Multicast Scope List option tells a client which scopes exist. RFC 2907 proposes a Multicast Scope Nesting State option that also says how those scopes nest. Clients can then choose scopes better for a session and build hierarchies of administratively scoped zones.
sections.eli5: A list of groups is useful. A list that also says which group is inside which is more useful, because you can start small and grow.

sections.title: The Split Horizon Problem and Expanding Scope Searches
sections.content:
Searching and localized recovery that rely on TTL scoping suffer when deployed widely. A requestor and a responder must each use a TTL large enough to reach the other. When they are many hops apart the TTL becomes large, and many receivers hear only the request or only the response. This is the split horizon effect.

Administrative scoping (RFC 2365) avoids this: routers stop packets in a range of multicast addresses at a configured perimeter, forming an administratively scoped zone. Routers can build and manage such zones with MZAP (RFC 2776), which can also tell whether zones nest.

With a hierarchy of zones, a requestor can run an expanding scope search. It starts at the smallest known scope and retransmits a small number of additional times at the same scope. If nothing answers, it moves to the next largest scope, and continues until it gets a response or reaches the largest legal scope for the session. Nodes that hear a response while waiting to send their own suppress it.
sections.eli5: Shouting louder and louder reaches lots of people who did not need to hear. It is better to ask in your own classroom first, then the whole school, then the town.

sections.title: Nesting State and the Scope List
sections.content:
Two scopes X and Y can be related in one of four ways: X nests inside Y, Y nests inside X, they do not nest (the overlap case), or they nest inside each other. The last case SHOULD be read as X and Y having exactly the same border, which does not make them the same scope because they may cover different multicast address ranges.

MADCAP servers MUST store this state and MUST allow it to be updated as the network changes. Each server SHOULD keep two pieces of state per pair, written X/Y for "X nests inside Y", each either true or false. Indeterminate state counts as false.

The Multicast Scope List option lists each visible scope as a tuple of Scope ID (the smallest address in its range), Last Address (the largest), TTL, and one or more language-specific names. The new option is OPTIONAL: servers MAY implement it. They learn nesting by static configuration or from a protocol such as MZAP.
sections.eli5: Two circles can be one inside the other, either way round, side by side overlapping, or exactly on top of each other. The server keeps a yes or no for each pair.

sections.title: The Bit-Packed Nesting Matrix
sections.content:
For n scopes there are n(n-1)/2 pairings, and the RFC counts n(n-1) pieces of nesting information. For efficiency and flexibility the option uses a bit-packed matrix. Row X and column Y hold the state X/Y: a 1 means the row scope nests inside the column scope, and a 0 means false or indeterminate. The diagonal is removed, since a scope compared with itself carries no information, and each row is zero-padded to the next byte boundary.

The RFC's example has seven scopes with nestings S1/S2, S2/S3, S2/S4, S3/S5, S4/S5, S5/S6 and S6/S7. Note that many more nesting relationships are implied by that set. The final representation is seven bytes, one per row.

The option depends on the Multicast Scope List option, because scope descriptions can change and the two must travel atomically. It MUST only be used in messages that carry the scope list option, specifically an ACK in response to GETINFO, and MUST NOT be included without it. A client wanting nesting lists both option codes in an Option Request option in a GETINFO message.
sections.eli5: Picture a grid of yes and no boxes, one row per group. Each row is squashed into a tiny number written in ones and zeros, so the whole grid takes very little space.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The option has four parts. Code is 16 bits and holds the option identifier 17. Len is 16 bits and gives the length of the option in bytes. Count is 8 bits and gives the number of zones in the matrix.

Count MUST be identical to the Count field in the preceding Multicast Scope List option. If it is not, the scope nesting information MUST be ignored. The Nest State Matrix is the compressed matrix derived as in the example, and for N scopes it is N times ceil((N-1)/8) bytes long. Its rows and columns follow the same order as the scopes in the Multicast Scope List option.
sections.eli5: The message starts with a label saying what it is, then how long it is, then how many groups there are, and then the grid. If the group count does not match the list, the grid is thrown away.

sections.title: Keeping Nesting State Current with Timers
sections.content:
Scope boundaries change when a network partitions or heals, is brought up, or a router is reconfigured. Servers MUST therefore track whether a nesting decision is still pending or definitive, whether a scope has been destroyed, and whether a boundary change has flipped a relationship. Two timers cover the first two: NEST_NO_DECISION_TIMER and ZONES_EXIST_TIMER.

When MZAP is used, servers eavesdrop on messages sent by Zone Border Routers. Zone Announcement Messages (ZAMs) show which scopes exist, and Not Inside Messages (NIMs) show which do not nest. When a NIM says X does not nest in Y, the server MUST set X/Y to false and restart NEST_NO_DECISION_TIMER for it. Until that timer expires, a server MUST NOT conclude that a scope nests within another.

If NEST_NO_DECISION_TIMER expires and no message has said X does not nest in Y, the server MUST conclude that X nests in Y and change X/Y from false to true. It then starts ZONES_EXIST_TIMER, which resets only when a ZAM has been received for both zones since the last restart. If that timer expires, the server SHOULD conclude one of the zones no longer exists and destroy both X/Y and Y/X state.
sections.eli5: The server assumes a group is inside another only after it has waited long enough without hearing "no". It keeps checking that both groups still exist, and forgets the pair if they go quiet.

sections.title: Security and Timer Constants
sections.content:
The option inherits the security concerns of MADCAP. If its contents were falsified, clients would be misinformed about nesting and would pick scopes in the wrong order. They would use larger scopes than necessary, flattening the hierarchy and cancelling its advantage. Protocols relying on the hierarchy would scale less well, but would not be prevented from working.

For the timers, the RFC says that with MZAP, NEST_NO_DECISION_TIMER should be greater than the MZAP NIM-INTERVAL plus 30%, which is 1800 + 30% = 2340 seconds (39 minutes). ZONES_EXIST_TIMER should be no less than the MZAP NIM-HOLDTIME, which has a default of 5460 seconds (91 minutes). IANA has assigned the option MADCAP option code 17.
sections.eli5: If someone lies about which group is inside which, computers shout to bigger crowds than needed. That is wasteful but not fatal.
